words.definition: the study of how scarce resources are allocated among competing uses
words.example: Economics examines choices about production, consumption and resource allocation.

words.definition: the study of environmental problems using economic concepts such as incentives, externalities and valuation
words.example: Environmental economics can compare the costs of pollution control with the benefits of cleaner air.

words.definition: an interdisciplinary approach that treats the economy as embedded within social and ecological systems
words.example: Ecological economics emphasizes biophysical limits to economic activity.

words.definition: a situation in which unregulated markets do not allocate resources in a socially efficient way
words.example: Air pollution is a market failure when health costs are not included in the price of fuel.

words.definition: a cost or benefit from an activity that affects third parties and is not fully reflected in market prices
words.example: Factory emissions create an externality when nearby residents bear health costs.

words.definition: an uncompensated harmful effect of an economic activity on others
words.example: Traffic congestion and air pollution are negative externalities of driving.

words.definition: an uncompensated beneficial effect of an activity on others
words.example: Restoring an urban wetland can create positive externalities such as flood protection and recreation.

words.definition: a good that is difficult to exclude people from using and is not substantially depleted by one person's use
words.example: A stable global climate has characteristics of a public good.

words.definition: overuse of a shared resource when individuals gain private benefits while costs are spread across all users
words.example: An open-access fishery can suffer a tragedy of the commons.

words.definition: assigning monetary estimates to goods, services or environmental benefits and costs
words.example: Economic valuation can estimate the benefits people receive from a wetland.

words.definition: a method comparing the monetary value of expected benefits with expected costs of a project or policy
words.example: Cost-benefit analysis can compare flood-defence options.

words.definition: the maximum amount a person would pay to obtain a benefit or avoid a loss
words.example: Surveys may estimate willingness to pay for cleaner river water.

words.definition: estimation of the economic value of benefits provided by ecosystems
words.example: Ecosystem service valuation can reveal the economic importance of mangrove storm protection.

words.definition: financial support that lowers the cost of producing or consuming a good or service
words.example: A subsidy can encourage households to install solar panels.

words.definition: a tax designed to make a polluter face the external social cost of an activity
words.example: A fuel charge based on pollution damage is a Pigouvian tax.

words.definition: a policy that sets an overall pollution limit and allows emission permits to be traded
words.japanese: キャップ・アンド・トレード
words.example: Cap-and-trade can create a market price for carbon emissions.

words.definition: misleading communication that makes an organization or product appear more environmentally responsible than it is
words.japanese: グリーンウォッシング
words.example: Vague claims of being “eco-friendly” without evidence may be greenwashing.

words.definition: the total monetary value of final goods and services produced within a country over a period
words.example: Gross domestic product can rise even while natural capital is being depleted.

words.definition: an adjusted measure of economic output that attempts to account for environmental degradation or resource depletion
words.example: Green GDP may subtract estimated pollution and resource-loss costs from conventional output.

words.definition: a welfare indicator that adjusts economic activity for social and environmental benefits and costs
words.example: The genuine progress indicator can fall when inequality and environmental damage rise.

words.definition: a framework aiming to meet human needs while remaining within ecological limits
words.example: Doughnut economics evaluates development between a social foundation and an ecological ceiling.

words.definition: an economic model designed to keep products and materials in use while reducing waste and virgin-resource extraction
words.example: Repair, remanufacturing and recycling are central to a circular economy.

words.definition: an economy seeking stable material and energy throughput rather than continuous physical growth
words.example: A steady-state economy emphasizes well-being without continual expansion of resource use.

words.definition: a planned reduction of resource and energy throughput in high-consumption economies while seeking social well-being and equity
words.example: Degrowth proposals often focus on reducing unnecessary consumption while strengthening public services.

words.definition: systematic measurement of stocks and changes in ecosystems and natural resources alongside economic accounts
words.example: Natural capital accounting can record forest loss that ordinary GDP ignores.
